detailed_answer:
Design choices. Quantile edges taken from the reference give roughly equal reference mass per bin, which copes with skewed features; the edges are frozen so every later window is compared on the same bins. np.unique collapses duplicate edges, so a feature with a large spike (say many zeros) simply ends up with fewer bins. If only one or two distinct edges survive (a constant, or a binary feature so imbalanced that the interpolated quantiles stay at 0 and 1; a 50/50 binary feature keeps an interior edge at 0.5) there are no interior edges, so the code falls back to one bin per distinct value plus open bins on both sides; otherwise any change would score 0. Searching only the interior edges sends values below the reference minimum to the first bin and values above its maximum to the last, so out-of-range data is counted rather than dropped. Proportions are floored at eps because (q - p) * log(q / p) is undefined when either proportion is 0.

The floor makes the output an artefact once a bin is empty. With a 20,000-row N(0,1) reference and 1,000 current values all equal to 5.0, the PSI was about 12.4 with eps=1e-6 and about 3.9 with eps=1e-2. Read such a value as 'enormous', not as a magnitude to compare across runs.

Why 200 rows and 40 bins is a bad signal: PSI is a sum over bins of sampling noise even without drift. A rough chi-square-style argument gives an expected null value near (B - 1) * (1/n + 1/m): for B=10 and n=m=200 that is 0.09, and a 300-repetition simulation with two samples from the same normal distribution gave a mean of 0.089 (sd 0.046). With 40 bins (about 5 expected rows per bin) the approximation breaks down and the simulated mean was 0.50 (sd 0.15). Commonly quoted rule-of-thumb cutoffs such as 0.1 and 0.25 are not statistical thresholds, and with 40 bins both would be exceeded in nearly every run with no change at all (a 2,000-run check gave 98% above 0.25). Remedies: fewer bins, more rows, a longer window, or calibrating the alert threshold against the noise floor measured on same-distribution splits.
practical_answer:
Reference implementation (this exact code was run on Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.13 with numpy, together with the test below):

```python
import numpy as np


def psi(reference, current, n_bins=10, eps=1e-4):
    """Population Stability Index with quantile bins fixed from `reference`.

    Out-of-range current values fall into the first/last bin. Bin
    proportions are floored at `eps` so an empty bin gives a large but
    finite term instead of log(0). NaN/inf are ignored (monitor the null
    rate separately); a constant or two-valued reference gets one bin per value.
    """
    ref = np.asarray(reference, dtype=float)
    cur = np.asarray(current, dtype=float)
    ref = ref[np.isfinite(ref)]
    cur = cur[np.isfinite(cur)]
    if ref.size == 0 or cur.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("reference and current need at least one finite value")
    edges = np.unique(np.quantile(ref, np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_bins + 1)))
    inner = edges[1:-1]
    if inner.size == 0:
        # constant or two-valued reference: give each value its own bin plus
        # an open bin on each side, so any change is still visible
        inner = np.unique(np.concatenate([edges, np.nextafter(edges, np.inf)]))
    ref_idx = np.searchsorted(inner, ref, side="right")
    cur_idx = np.searchsorted(inner, cur, side="right")
    k = inner.size + 1
    p = np.bincount(ref_idx, minlength=k) / ref.size
    q = np.bincount(cur_idx, minlength=k) / cur.size
    p = np.maximum(p, eps)
    q = np.maximum(q, eps)
    return float(np.sum((q - p) * np.log(q / p)))
```

Suggested checks, all asserted in the recorded test: a constant or binary reference still registers a shift (constant reference against 9.0 gives more than 5, binary 50/50 against all ones more than 1) and NaNs are ignored; PSI of a sample against itself is exactly 0; two independent 20,000-row normal samples give less than 0.01; a 0.5 sd mean shift gives about 0.23; the all-5.0 case grows as eps shrinks; and the null PSI with 40 bins is more than three times the null PSI with 10 bins at n=200.

Operational recipe: before choosing an alert level for a feature, draw 100 pairs of non-overlapping windows of your production window size from a known-stable period (on the real time axis, so autocorrelation and weekly effects are included), compute PSI on each pair at your production bin count, and set the alert above a high percentile of that null distribution, not at a textbook constant.

Do not retrain yet; treat both as data-quality incidents until proven otherwise.

txn_amount: a PSI of 8.3 means essentially all current values fall in bins that held little reference mass. A change of units by a large factor such as 100 does exactly that for a narrowly spread amount distribution; with a wider spread the PSI is lower (about 4 for a lognormal with sigma 2) but still far above any threshold. In a simulation (50,000 lognormal amounts each side), multiplying every value by 100, as dollars-to-cents would, gave PSI about 8.2 with 10 quantile bins and eps=1e-4 (the ceiling for that setup is about 8.3) while two plain samples gave about 0.0003 (lognormal with sigma 1). The collapsed scores are most likely a consequence: the model is probably being fed out-of-support inputs (confirm by re-scoring a sample with the amounts rescaled). Fix at the source (or add an explicit conversion in the feature pipeline), backfill or mark the affected window, and exclude it from training data. Retraining on a mix of units would bake the bug into the model.

discount_pct: a null-to-zero spike moves about 9% of the mass into the lowest bin. detailed_answer:
Start from why it is noisy. With 120 features tested at p < 0.01, even if nothing changes you expect 120 x 0.01 = 1.2 false hits per day, and if the tests were independent the chance of at least one hit is 1 - 0.99^120, about 70%. Correlated features change that arithmetic but not the conclusion. In addition, with large daily volumes a p-value flags differences far too small to matter, so alerts are dominated by statistical significance rather than importance.

Principles for the redesign:
1. Alert on model-level symptoms and hard data-quality invariants first. The model's output distribution (score histogram, positive rate), data-quality invariants (schema, null rate, range) and, when available, quality proxies are what someone should be paged for. Per-feature distribution changes are diagnostic detail.
2. Use an effect size, not a p-value, and set thresholds from the metric's own history (for example a high percentile of the last 60-90 daily values, compared on the same weekday where there is weekly seasonality). The ML Test Score paper notes that alert thresholds need careful tuning to balance false positives against false negatives.
3. Require persistence: fire only if the condition holds for k of the last n windows, except for hard failures such as schema violations.
4. Tier the severity by feature importance and failure type, and route each tier to an owner.
5. Review the alerts: track which were actionable and retire or retune rules that never lead to action. Sculley et al. make a related point about action limits on a system's real-world actions: they should be broad enough not to trigger spuriously, and when one trips an alert should lead to investigation.

This design also fixes the missed incident: a null-rate regression becomes a data-quality rule with its own absolute band instead of one of 120 anonymous drift hits.
practical_answer:
Worked tier table for this model (illustrative values, tune on your history):
- Page (owner on call): schema or type violation; null rate of any of the top 10 features above its 90-day maximum by more than a set margin for 2 consecutive windows (compute these data-quality checks hourly, so a regression pages within hours rather than after two daily runs); score-distribution PSI above its own 99th-percentile historical value for 2 consecutive windows (a model-output symptom; page on it only if replaying past incidents shows it tracks quality, otherwise treat it as a ticket-level signal like other drift statistics; per-feature drift metrics stay at ticket or dashboard level).
- Ticket (next business day): null rate of any other feature above its 90-day maximum by more than a set margin; any single feature's drift metric above its own 99th-percentile history on 3 of the last 5 days; or the number of drifted features above its usual band.
- Dashboard only: everything else, with no notification.

Intended result with these rules (verify by replaying the last 90 days of metrics through them before enabling paging): a quiet channel on normal days, one page for the null-rate class of incident, and a weekly review of ticket outcomes. Each alert carries the metric value, its historical band, a link to the slice breakdown and the runbook step, so the receiver can decide quickly.

answer:
The storm is most likely a sample-size effect rather than a bug (rule out a systematic logging difference between reference and yesterday). A KS p-value answers 'is there any difference between the two distributions?', and with a million rows per side almost any real difference, however small, is significant. In a simulation with two N(0,1) samples of 1,000,000 rows where one was shifted by 0.01 standard deviations, the KS statistic was about 0.004 (0.0035 to 0.0055 over eight seeds) and the p-value between about 1e-5 and 1e-13, far below 0.05 every time, while PSI with 10 bins was about 0.0001. At the other extreme, 1,000 rows per side with a 0.3 sd shift gave, in one draw, KS statistic 0.14 (p about 8e-9) and PSI about 0.10 (PSI varied roughly 0.07 to 0.16 across draws). So p-values track evidence, not size.

What each measures. SciPy documents the KS statistic as the maximum absolute difference between the two empirical CDFs, with a null hypothesis of identical distributions, and assumes continuous inputs. The statistic itself is a bounded effect size and is the thing to threshold (ideally against its historical variation). PSI is not a test: it bins the data, and sums (q - p) * log(q / p) over bins, so it depends on the bin count and any empty-bin floor, is sensitive to where mass moves between bins, and has a noise floor of roughly (B - 1) * (1/n + 1/m).

Caveats. KS on features with many ties (spikes at 0, integer counts, sentinel values) violates the continuity assumption, so use PSI or a chi-square-type comparison on bins or categories instead. KS is often more sensitive to changes in the bulk of the distribution than to far tails, so pair it with min/max or tail-quantile checks when tails matter.

Neither tells you whether the model cares: that needs feature importance, prediction drift, and eventually labels. Neither sees changes in joint structure (correlations) when marginals stay the same, and neither reports why the shift happened, such as a data-quality bug.

answer:
Treat the dashboard as a lead, not a verdict. Feature drift is harmless when the model's behaviour on the new inputs is still what it learned; it is harmful when the inputs leave the region where the model is reliable or when the input-to-label relationship has changed. Without labels you can test the first part cheaply.

Triage steps:
1. Weight by importance. Rank the 14 drifted features by the model's importance (permutation importance on labelled validation data, or attribution mass such as mean absolute SHAP on a recent sample). Drift in low-importance or redundant features matters little.
2. Counterfactual replacement. Re-score a recent sample after replacing each drifted feature (or the group) with values resampled from the reference. Independent resampling breaks correlations with the other features, so treat the result as a sensitivity check, not an exact estimate. If the scores barely move, the drift is not driving predictions; if they move a lot, find out in which direction.
3. Support check. What fraction of current rows lie outside the training range or in sparsely populated regions? Inputs inside the training support are interpolation; far outside they are extrapolation, where tree-based models predict a constant beyond the observed range and neural nets can behave unpredictably.
4. Slice the output. Check score distributions and queue rates for campaign-acquired cohorts vs the rest, since an unchanged aggregate can hide a changed slice.
5. Get cheap labels. Have analysts review a small random sample of campaign traffic, or use early proxies such as confirmed customer disputes.

What changes the answer: scores shifting, rows outside support, or analyst labels disagreeing with the model are signs of possible harm. Unchanged scores do not rule out concept drift, because the model can still output the same scores for inputs whose fraud rate changed; only labels settle that.

Retraining tonight on a few days of campaign-skewed data risks fitting a transient and makes it harder to attribute any change. Prefer monitoring, targeted checks and a scheduled retrain once labels mature.

Dilution. In a simulation of 100,000 rows with 10% from the new market, basket_value shifted from N(50, 10) to N(80, 10) in that market only. Fix: compute the drift and quality metrics per slice as well as overall. The ML Test Score paper makes a parallel point for prediction bias: models should have zero bias in aggregate and on slices.

Costs and limits:
- Multiplicity: F features x S slices x metrics multiplies the false-alarm opportunities, so use effect-size thresholds, persistence and a ranking by slice size times severity rather than paging on each pair.
- Sample size: a small slice has a high noise floor of roughly (B - 1) * (1/n + 1/m) for PSI, so enforce a minimum row count and use longer windows for small slices, or sample them at a higher rate.
- Interpretation: when the aggregate drifts but each slice is stable, the cause is a mix shift (traffic composition changed). That can be harmless if the model performs well in each slice; compare aggregate and per-slice results to tell the two cases apart.
- New slices that did not exist at training time cannot appear in a reference, so also alert on previously unseen category values and sharp changes in slice share.

detailed_answer:
Separate three needs, because they have different cost profiles.

1. Always-on aggregates, computed in the stream with no raw rows retained: request counts, null and zero rates, min/max, quantile sketches or histograms on the frozen reference bin edges, score histograms, category counts, per slice and per model version. Counters and histograms are exact over all traffic (quantile sketches are approximate) and tiny, and they serve the data-quality and drift dashboards.

2. A sampled set of raw feature rows for investigation, drift tests that need raw values, and the label join. Sample deterministically from a hash of the request ID, for example keep the row if a stable hash of the ID (for example SHA-256 or xxHash, not Python's salted built-in hash()) mod 10,000 is below 100 for a 1% rate. The decision is reproducible, uncorrelated with feature values as long as request IDs are not derived from user or feature data, and needs no coordination, and the same ID can later be joined to labels. Always store the sampling rate or weight on each row so estimates can be re-weighted.

3. Higher or full capture where rarity matters: errors, low-confidence scores and small but important slices.

Sizing. At 1%, 2,000,000 x 0.01 = 20,000 rows a day, about 80 MB at 4 KB instead of 8 GB. The PSI noise floor is roughly (B - 1) * (1/n + 1/m); with B=10, a 100,000-row reference and 20,000 daily rows, that is 9 x (0.00001 + 0.00005), about 0.0005, negligible. But the 0.5% slice gets only 2,000,000 x 0.005 x 0.01 = 100 rows a day, about 4 per hour, which is useless; even 50 rows gives roughly 9 x (0.00001 + 0.02), about 0.18 (the approximation is rough at so few rows; a simulation gave roughly 0.2 to 0.25), above a typical 0.1 line with no drift at all. So the slice should be covered at 100%, either by its streamed per-slice histograms (item 1) or by raw capture when rows are needed for investigation, which is 10,000 rows a day, about 417 an hour on average (fewer overnight, where the floor is higher), and the hourly floor becomes about 9 x (0.00001 + 1/417), about 0.02 (assuming a 100,000-row reference for the slice; if the slice reference holds only its own 0.5% share, about 500 rows, the floor is 9 x (1/500 + 1/417), about 0.04).

Privacy: log the model's input features rather than raw free text or identifiers where possible, pseudonymise IDs, and set retention limits; what is permitted depends on jurisdiction and legal advice.
practical_answer:
Concrete policy for this service (illustrative):
- Stream job: per-hour counters and histograms for all 2M requests/day, retained for the long term.
- Raw sample: 1% by request-ID hash, retained for a limited period that must still exceed the longest label delay (weeks), or the join has nothing to attach to, with the sampling rate stored per row.
- Slice rule: 100% of the 0.5% slice, plus 100% of errors and of scores in the top uncertain band; each row tagged with its sampling weight (1 for 100%, 100 for the 1% sample). Run drift tests and population estimates on the uniform hash sample (or on the union with inverse-inclusion-probability weights), never on the mixed set unweighted.
- Label join: key on request ID; labels arriving weeks later attach to whichever rows were kept, so performance estimates for the general population use the weighted 1% sample.

Validation before trusting it: for two or three days, log everything once (under a short retention, with security sign-off), then compare the sampled histograms and null rates with the full ones. For each feature, PSI between the 1% sample and the full data should sit near the noise floor computed above (a few 0.0001s); if a feature stands out, the sampling key is correlated with something. Repeat the check after any change to the ID format.

answer:
Each reference answers a different question, so use two.

(A) Training set: answers 'how far is today from what the model learned?', which is the question that matters for model validity. Weekly seasonality still causes recurring weekend alarms when a single day is compared with the all-days training mixture, unless you compare like with like (same weekday or weekday-adjusted), but it does catch the creep: after 60 days the mean has moved 60 x 0.05 = 3 sd. Downsides: once the shift is real it stays red permanently and says nothing about when it started.

(B) Yesterday: compares Monday to Sunday, so the weekly cycle produces false alarms every week. It is also nearly blind to the creep: a day-over-day change of 0.05 sd is smaller than the weekly swing (unless the standard deviation exceeds about five times the mean) and, unless daily volume is large (about 7,200 rows per day are needed to see it at 3 standard errors), within sampling noise.

(C) Pooled previous 7 days: the reference averages out the weekly cycle, but today is a single day, so it is still compared with a weekly mixture. With weekends 25% higher, the weekly average is about 7% above a weekday level, so a weekend day sits about 17% above the pool and a weekday about 7% below it; seasonal false alarms remain unless today is also a 7-day window or the comparison is weekday-adjusted. Its lag is also large: the average age of the pooled days is (1 + ... + 7) / 7 = 4 days, so under steady creep today sits about 4 x 0.05 = 0.2 sd above the reference. That is a constant small offset, easy to miss when seasonal swings and alert tolerances are of similar size, and it does not accumulate.

(D) Same weekday, previous 4 weeks: removes the weekday effect if the weekly pattern is stable; the average age is (7 + 14 + 21 + 28) / 4 = 17.5 days, so the creep offset is about 17.5 x 0.05 = 0.875 sd, much more visible, though each weekday sample is only 4 pooled days, so its noise floor is higher than C's 7-day pool (4 days of rows instead of 7) and holidays contaminate it.

Recommendation: keep a seasonal-aware rolling reference (D, or C with weekday adjustment) to catch recent changes with few false alarms, plus a fixed training reference tracked as a slowly moving 'distance from training' trend with a staleness limit that triggers a retrain review. Reset the fixed reference only when you retrain. Compare both against historical variability, not a constant threshold.

concise_answer: Continuous training (CT) is the automated retraining, validation and serving of models in response to triggers such as a schedule, new data, performance decay or data-distribution change. CI/CD ships changes to code. CT adds an ML-specific loop where the data, not the code, changes and the model must be rebuilt, which needs data validation before training and model validation before release.
detailed_answer:
In application software, behaviour changes only when someone changes the code, so CI/CD (build, test, deploy) is enough to keep production current. In an ML system the model is a product of code plus data, so the same code can yield a different, and eventually staler, model as the world and the data change. Continuous training automates that second loop: a pipeline that can be triggered repeatedly, retrains the model, checks it and, if it passes, hands it to deployment. Google's MLOps architecture guidance describes CT as a property unique to ML systems concerned with automatically retraining and serving models, and lists triggers such as a schedule, availability of new training data, performance degradation and significant changes in data distributions.

Differences from code CI/CD:
- What is tested: besides code and components, CI/CD for ML also covers data (schema, distribution checks) and models (quality against a baseline).
- Two extra gates: data validation before training decides whether it is worth, or safe, to retrain; model validation after training decides whether the new model may replace the current one.
- Artifacts: the pipeline must record the data version, features, parameters and metrics, since the result is not reproducible from code alone.
- Triggers: not only commits but also time, data arrival and monitoring signals.

Common pitfalls: 'continuous' does not mean retraining all the time. Retraining has cost and risk, so the trigger policy and the validation gates matter more than the frequency. Automating retraining without data validation and model validation simply automates the production of bad models. CT also does not replace CI/CD: pipeline code still needs ordinary testing and deployment.

detailed_answer:
This is a selection-bias feedback loop. Outcomes (repayment or default) are observed only for approved applicants, so the training set is truncated to people the previous model already liked. The model never sees what happens to rejected applicants, cannot learn that some of them would have repaid, and is evaluated on a population it pre-filtered. Each retrain makes the model better at ranking within the approved region and leaves its behaviour outside that region untested. Sculley et al. describe the general case: a model may directly influence the selection of its own future training data.

Why the offline numbers mislead: they are computed on loans the model chose, where its scores are concentrated and the outcome range is narrow, so improvements say little about the rejected 60%, and the extra confidence never gets challenged.

Redesign:
- Exploration: approve a small random sample of applicants who would have been rejected, ideally concentrated near the threshold, record the approval probability (propensity) and the outcome. This gives unbiased labels for a part of the rejected region at a known business cost.
- Weighting: use inverse-propensity weights in training and evaluation so that the explored cases represent the rejected population they were drawn from.
- Evaluation: judge challengers on the exploration slice and on any data from policy-independent sources, not on the approved set alone.
- Logging: store the model version, score, threshold and decision with every application so you can tell how the data was selected.
- Alternatives such as reject inference (imputing outcomes for rejected applicants) rely on modelling assumptions and are best treated as supplementary, not as a replacement for real outcomes.

Exploration has a direct cost and may need risk and compliance approval; what is allowed depends on jurisdiction and legal advice.
practical_answer:
Worked sizing for the exploration slice (illustrative): of 50,000 monthly applications, 60% are rejected, which is 30,000. Randomly approve 2% of the rejected applicants whose score is within a band below the threshold. If the band covers all rejected applicants that is 600 loans a month, each carrying weight 1 / 0.02 = 50 in training and evaluation (it stands for 50 rejected applicants). If 15% of those loans default, that is about 90 observed defaults a month, so the slice supports coarse estimates but not fine-grained slicing; you would accumulate several months or concentrate the band closer to the threshold to get more labels where the decision is closest.

Promotion rule to add to the pipeline: a challenger is promoted only if it is not worse than the champion on the weighted exploration slice (with an interval, not a point estimate) as well as on the approved set. Keep the exploration budget capped, tracked as an explicit cost, and reviewed by risk owners.

answer:
The root problem is a pipeline that treats every drift alarm as a reason to learn and uses the same possibly corrupted data to train and to judge. Guardrails, in pipeline order:

1. Trigger: separate data-quality alerts (null/zero rate, range, schema) from distribution drift. A data-quality failure should block automated retraining and go to the data owner, not start it. Add persistence (the condition holds for several windows) and a cooldown or maximum retrains per period, so a flapping alarm cannot cause a chain of retrains.

2. Data validation before training: Google's MLOps guidance states that data validation is required before training to decide whether to retrain. Run it on the whole training window: schema, null and zero rates, ranges, row counts and label rates compared with their usual bands. Quarantine bad partitions (here the six hours) instead of training on them, and fail the run if the failures are too large.

3. Trusted evaluation data: the holdout must pass the same validation and should not be allowed to share the defect that the training data had. Prefer a time-based holdout of validated data, plus a fixed, curated reference set that rarely changes, so a corrupted recent window cannot grade itself.

4. Model validation after training: besides AUC against the champion, compare the new model's predictions against the champion's on the trusted set and on the champion's slices, and bound the change. Sculley et al. suggest action limits on a system's real-world actions as sanity checks that are broad enough not to trigger spuriously; a similar bound on champion/challenger change (a sudden large shift in score distribution or in the importance of income) should stop promotion.

5. Approval and rollout: require human approval when the model affects money or when the behaviour change exceeds a limit, and release through a staged rollout with a rollback path.

6. Record data versions and excluded partitions so the incident can be audited.

Guardrails 1 and 2 alone would very likely have stopped this incident; the later layers are defence in depth, covering a missed quality check, a corrupted holdout, or a model that passes AUC but behaves abnormally.

answer:
Warm start trades compute for risks that accumulate silently.

Benefits: 40 minutes vs 14 hours a day, quicker adaptation to recent changes, and a smaller gap between new data arriving and the model reflecting it. Rules of Machine Learning (Rule 8) advises measuring how much performance degrades as a model ages, which tells you how much freshness is worth.

Risks:
- Recency bias and forgetting: training only on the last day can overwrite patterns that a 180-day window contains, such as weekly cycles, rare seasonal behaviour or small segments absent yesterday. A single day also over-represents one weekday.
- Error persistence: a bad day (bug, outage, bot traffic) leaves a trace in the weights that later updates only gradually dilute, whereas in a sliding-window retrain the bad day leaves the window after 180 days, or can be dropped at once from the data.
- Reproducibility and lineage: the model is a function of the whole chain of updates, so 'this code plus this data version' no longer recreates it, and a defective link cannot be undone without going back to an earlier checkpoint.
- Optimiser and schedule effects: learning rate schedules and optimiser state must be handled deliberately, and some model families do not support clean continuation (for example, some tree libraries can continue boosting from an existing model while others only refit, so check the library's documented behaviour).

A common compromise: warm-start daily from the last full-retrain checkpoint, possibly mixing in a replay sample of older data, and do a full retrain weekly, which bounds drift between the two and resets accumulated error.

Decide empirically with a rolling-origin backtest over the last 60 days: for each day, produce both variants using only data available then (at 14 hours per full retrain, 60 daily full retrains is costly, so run the warm-start chain on consecutive days from one full-retrain checkpoint, since it is cheap at about 40 minutes a day and its errors accumulate along the chain, and compute the full-retrain baseline only on a sample of 10 to 15 of those days or on a subsampled dataset), score both on the same following window, and compare overall and by slice, along with the cost and day-to-day stability (visible in full for the warm-start chain, only coarsely for the sampled full retrains). Include a day with a deliberately injected bad batch to see how long each variant needs to recover. If warm-start is within noise of the full retrain on every slice and recovers, its cost advantage justifies it.

Redeploying v11 restores one artifact, not the system. Check these:

1. Everything that was released with v12. Decision thresholds, calibration layers, feature definitions, post-processing rules and config changed with v12 must go back too, or v11 runs with v12's cut-offs. Confirm that v11 still loads, that the features it expects are still produced in the online path, and that its dependencies remain deployed.
2. The data produced in Tuesday to Thursday. For those two days the system's decisions came from v12, so any outcomes (clicks, purchases, labels) were shaped by it. If v12 behaved badly, logs from that period may be biased or may carry unusual behaviour. Tag all logs with model version, and exclude or down-weight the v12 window when building the next training set, particularly for feedback-loop-prone systems. Keep the logs, since they are the evidence for the post-mortem.
3. The retrain trigger. Whatever fired the pipeline that produced v12 will probably fire again. Pause automatic promotion (or the trigger) until you know why v12 was worse; otherwise the pipeline will re-ship a similar model on its next run.
4. Staleness. v11 is older than v12. Record it in the registry as the current production model, check its freshness against what the business accepts, and plan the next candidate rather than letting v11 age silently.
5. The gate that failed. Determine why offline evaluation approved a model that hurt online conversion (a metric not aligned with conversions, a slice not evaluated, a holdout not representative, or a feature unavailable or different online) and add a check that would have caught it. Add the online guardrail metric that detected it to the automated rollback policy.
6. Evidence trail. The registry should show v12's status, the rollback reason, who approved it and the metrics before and after, so the decision is auditable.

Time to detection matters: partial exposure, like a canary, would have limited the damage to a small share of traffic.

detailed_answer:
Aggregate AUC averages over the whole population, so a retrained model can score higher while becoming sensitive to something it should ignore, or while reversing a relationship the business relies on. Behavioural tests state expectations about how the score should respond to controlled input changes and measure how often the model breaks them.

Three useful families. Invariance: change an input that should not matter (an identifier hash, name casing, a unit-preserving rewrite) and the score should stay within a small tolerance; failures point to identifier leakage or a proxy the model should not use. Directional expectation: change an input in a direction whose effect is known (one more missed payment, all else equal) and the score should not move the other way. Minimum functionality: a small curated set of cases with an obvious right answer.

Design choices. Run the checks on real, representative rows, change one column at a time on a copy of the data (never mutate the evaluation set in place), and report a failure rate, not just the first failure. Calibrate invariance tolerances empirically: run the check on the current production model (and on a retrain with a different seed) and set tol just above the float noise and routine score movement they show, then fix tol before looking at the candidate; for invariance checks the allowed failure rate is typically set at or near zero. For directional checks on a model with no monotonic constraints, demanding exactly zero is often unrealistic: an unconstrained tree ensemble or neural network fits whatever the noisy data and feature interactions support, so the response along one feature can dip locally even when the overall trend is monotone. A pragmatic gate compares the candidate's failure rate with the current production model's and blocks on a clear regression. If the business needs a guarantee, enforce it in training (monotonic constraints, where the library supports them) and keep the test as a guard. Use realistic step sizes inside the training range, and fix thresholds before looking at the candidate's results.

Pitfalls: a perturbation that leaves values unchanged (the test can never fail), checks run on a tiny sample, and treating a green behavioural report as proof of fairness or correctness; it covers only the behaviours you thought to write down.
practical_answer:
Reference implementation (numpy only):

```python
import numpy as np


def _as_float(X):
    """Float matrix (integer input is cast so a fractional step is not truncated; float32 stays float32)."""
    X = np.asarray(X)
    return X if X.dtype.kind == "f" else X.astype(float)


def invariance_failures(predict, X, col, perturb, tol=0.01):
    """Row indices where changing column `col` with perturb() moves the score by more than tol (a NaN score counts as a failure)."""
    X = _as_float(X)
    X2 = X.copy()
    X2[:, col] = perturb(X[:, col].copy())
    return np.flatnonzero(~(np.abs(predict(X2) - predict(X)) <= tol))


def directional_failures(predict, X, col, step, direction=1, tol=1e-9):
    """Row indices where adding `step` to column `col` moves the score against `direction` (+1 or -1); NaN scores count as failures."""
    X = _as_float(X)
    X2 = X.copy()
    X2[:, col] = X[:, col] + step
    delta = (predict(X2) - predict(X)) * direction
    return np.flatnonzero(~(delta >= -tol))


def behavioural_report(predict, X, checks, max_fail_rate):
    """checks: name -> function(predict, X) returning failing row indices. Returns (passed, rates)."""
    rates = {name: len(fn(predict, X)) / len(X) for name, fn in checks.items()}
    passed = all(rates[name] <= max_fail_rate[name] for name in checks)
    return passed, rates
```

What the executed test showed: with a correct toy logistic model, all three failure rates are 0.0. With the sign of the missed-payments weight flipped, the directional check fails on 100% of the 500 rows while both invariance checks stay at 0.0. With a model that gives postcode_hash a weight of 0.8, the postcode invariance check fails on 52.4% of rows while the customer-hash check remains 0.0, so each defect trips only its own check. Further assertions check that integer-typed matrices are perturbed correctly (they are cast to float first), float32 input stays float32 (no cast noise), a NaN score counts as a failure rather than a silent pass, and a perturb function that mutates its argument in place can neither corrupt X nor hide the failure.

Wiring: define the checks next to the model code, run them in the promotion pipeline on the candidate and the production model with the same rows, and store both failure-rate tables with the run so a reviewer can see the delta.

detailed_answer:
The test is a per-row comparison of two timestamps: a feature value is point-in-time correct for a training row only if it was computed at or before the moment the prediction would have been made (prediction_ts). Grouping by feature turns that into an audit that shows which feature is the problem and how bad it is. Comparing feature_ts with label_ts (assuming label_ts is never earlier than prediction_ts, so rows_after_label is a subset of rows_from_future) separates two different failures: a value that is later than prediction_ts but earlier than the label is a point-in-time violation (the live system could not have known it), while a value later than label_ts may be derived from the outcome itself, which is target leakage proper.

On the example run (SQLite dialect, executed in the test on 4 training rows and 12 feature values, where refund_flag is stamped between 12 hours and about 20 days after prediction time and days_since_login is stamped 23:59 on the prediction day for three of the four rows): refund_flag has all 4 rows from the future, up to 470 hours ahead, and all 4 are after the label time, so it is almost certainly computed from the outcome and should be removed or rebuilt. days_since_login has 3 of 4 rows (share 0.75) from the future by at most 15 hours and none after the label: it is a nightly snapshot stamped at the end of the day and joined by date, so it leaks a few hours of future activity; the fix is an as-of join (latest value with feature_ts <= prediction_ts) or a snapshot taken before prediction time. orders_30d does not appear because every value precedes its prediction time.

Limits. The query trusts feature_ts. If the stamp is the event time rather than the time the data was actually available, late-arriving records still leak (the failure in a backfill over records that arrived days late). Features with no timestamp, rows whose label_ts is NULL (they are never counted in rows_after_label), leakage that is not temporal (duplicate entities across train and validation, aggregates computed over the full dataset), and clock or timezone mixing are not caught. ISO-8601 text compares correctly as strings only if every value uses the same format and timezone.

The query (SQLite dialect; ISO-8601 timestamps; run in the test (code.test) against a four-row in-memory dataset):

```sql
SELECT f.feature,
       COUNT(*) AS n_rows,
       SUM(CASE WHEN f.feature_ts > r.prediction_ts THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS rows_from_future,
       ROUND(1.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN f.feature_ts > r.prediction_ts THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS future_share,
       ROUND(MAX((julianday(f.feature_ts) - julianday(r.prediction_ts)) * 24), 1) AS max_hours_ahead,
       SUM(CASE WHEN f.feature_ts > r.label_ts THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS rows_after_label
FROM training_rows AS r
JOIN training_features AS f ON f.row_id = r.row_id
GROUP BY f.feature
HAVING rows_from_future > 0
ORDER BY future_share DESC, f.feature;
```

detailed_answer:
Each of the four things you found is a way for a check to be vacuous, and together they explain a nine-month green streak.

1. The baseline is the data under test. If expected statistics are recomputed from the candidate table, the candidate always matches itself. Expectations must come from a frozen, reviewed reference (a schema and statistics from a known-good training set or recent accepted runs), versioned separately from the data.
2. Slices come from the data. Looping over regions present in the table means a region that disappears is never visited. The list of required slices must come from configuration (or the previous accepted run), and a required slice with zero rows, or a row count far below its expected range, is a failure.
3. NaN defeats comparisons. In Python (and IEEE floating point) any ordered comparison with NaN is False, so `NaN > limit` never fails. An empty group's mean is NaN, so the check passes exactly when the data is missing. Write checks in the form `if not (value <= limit): fail`, so NaN fails, and treat 'no rows' as its own error.
4. Failures are not propagated. If violations are only logged, or the job's status depends solely on exceptions, the orchestrator never sees a problem. Return a non-zero status or raise when any error-severity check fails, and let warnings go to a report.

A related trap is the all-passed-of-nothing case: `all([])` is True, so an empty table or zero checks executed looks healthy. Count the checks that actually ran and alert if that number drops.

A feature that is 100% null should fail any null-rate limit; here it can still slip through when the limit is judged against the self-derived baseline, or when rows with nulls were dropped before the statistic was computed. The fix is not complete until the validator has been shown to fail on known-bad input.
practical_answer:
Test the validator as you would test any safety mechanism, with a small suite of deliberately broken batches that must each return a failure:

1. Dropped slice: remove all 'EU' rows from a copy of a good table; expect a 'required slice missing' error.
2. Fully null feature: set one feature to None for every row; expect a null-rate error.
3. Empty table and zero-row slice: expect an explicit error, not a pass.
4. NaN statistic: force a NaN mean; expect a failure, not a pass.
5. Self-comparison: pass the candidate as its own reference and confirm the run is refused, or that the reference is read from a different frozen artifact.
6. Orchestration: make one check fail and assert the task exit status is non-zero and downstream tasks do not run.

Add two run-time guards: record 'checks executed' and 'slices evaluated' with each run and alert if either falls below the configured minimum, and run the broken-batch suite in CI whenever the validator changes. A rule of thumb from the Rules of Machine Learning is to test getting data into the algorithm, for example checking that columns that should be populated are populated; the suite above checks that your checker does so.

concise_answer: Inference only records what one snapshot looked like, so it freezes accidents as rules. Review observed ranges, category sets, 'required' flags, null tolerances and types, then add what only domain knowledge provides: valid ranges, units, cross-column constraints, severity (error vs warn), skew/drift thresholds based on measured natural variation, and an owner and versioning. Also check the snapshot itself was healthy.
detailed_answer:
An inferred schema is a description of the data it was computed from, not a statement of what valid data is. Inference tools differ in how aggressively they generalise from a snapshot; TensorFlow Data Validation's documentation, for example, says it uses conservative heuristics and strongly advises reviewing the inferred schema and refining it to capture domain knowledge its heuristics may have missed. Treating the output as final produces both failure modes in the question.

What to review. Where a tool derives numeric ranges from observed min and max (not every tool does), those ranges will reject a legitimately larger order next month and accept a value that is wrong but inside last month's range. Category sets taken from observed values flag every new product code (noise) and may omit rare valid ones. 'Required' or 'present in 100% of rows' is often just what happened to be true. Null tolerances set at the observed rate bake in any existing bug; if 4% of a feature was null because of a broken join, the schema now calls that normal. Types can be inferred too narrowly (an integer-looking ID that is really a string).

What to add. Valid ranges and units from the business (age between 0 and a plausible maximum, currency in a fixed unit), relationships across columns (end time not before start time), which checks are errors that block and which are warnings, and comparison thresholds for skew and drift. Set those thresholds from how much the statistic naturally varies between healthy days, not from zero, or the check will fire constantly. Give the schema an owner, store it in version control, and require review for changes so that relaxing it is a visible decision.

Finally, validate the baseline: run the schema over several past periods, including a known-bad one, to confirm it passes the good periods and fails the bad. The ML Test Score rubric lists capturing feature expectations in a schema, and checking that data invariants hold in both training and serving inputs, as separate items.

detailed_answer:
The attack path is: stolen notebook credentials, write access to the shared bucket or registry alias, then a serving process that loads the artifact. Many model formats are code-bearing: Python's pickle documentation warns that unpickling can execute arbitrary code and that data that could have come from an untrusted source or been tampered with must never be unpickled. So the controls are those of any software supply chain.

1. Identities and least privilege. Experiments run under per-user identities that write only to an experiment namespace; only the pipeline's service identity registers a model version; moving the production alias is a separate role needing approval by someone other than the author, after automated gates (tests, dependency scan, model card). The serving identity is read-only on approved locations. Protects against: a stolen notebook token writing to the production path or moving the alias. If that identity can launch pipeline jobs it can still get a malicious artifact registered, so approval and loader hardening carry that case. Does not protect against: an insider who holds the promotion role.
2. Integrity. At registration the pipeline records a content digest (and ideally signs it with a key the notebooks cannot reach); serving verifies the digest before deserialising. Protects against: swapped or tampered files in the bucket. Does not protect against: a malicious artifact that was legitimately produced and registered, and a digest is only as trustworthy as the registry record, so restrict registry writes.
3. Loader hardening. Prefer data-only formats where the model type allows; otherwise treat loading as running untrusted code: no network egress, read-only filesystem, non-root, minimal secrets in the process. Protects against: a payload that gets past the other controls spreading beyond the loader (exfiltration, lateral movement). Does not protect against: the model's own malicious behaviour or an attacker who controls the data the loader legitimately reads.
4. Dependencies and images. Lock files with hashes, an internal package mirror, vulnerability and license scanning in CI, base images pinned by digest and rebuilt on a schedule. Protects against: packages whose contents change after you locked them, typosquatted names when the internal mirror serves only reviewed packages, and silent upstream base-image changes. Does not protect against: a malicious or vulnerable version you pinned on purpose, or a flaw the scanner does not yet know.
5. Audit. Immutable log of who registered, approved and moved each alias, linked to run, code commit and data version, with an alert on every production-alias move. Protects against: undetected or deniable promotions and slow forensics. Does not protect against: the attack itself, since it detects and attributes after the fact.

Residual risk: poisoned data or a backdoored model behaves as designed but maliciously, so behavioural validation still matters.
practical_answer:
A minimal digest check that serving runs before it deserialises anything; the expected digest comes from the registry record written by the pipeline identity, never from the bucket next to the file:

```python
import hashlib
import hmac


def sha256_file(path, chunk_size=1 << 20):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for block in iter(lambda: f.read(chunk_size), b""):
            h.update(block)
    return h.hexdigest()


def verify_artifact(path, expected_sha256):
    """Raise before any deserialisation if the file is not byte-identical to what the registry recorded."""
    actual = sha256_file(path)
    if not hmac.compare_digest(actual, expected_sha256.strip().lower()):
        raise ValueError(f"artifact digest mismatch: expected {expected_sha256[:12]}..., got {actual[:12]}...")
    return actual
```

Procedure around it: (1) the pipeline computes sha256 when it registers the version and stores it with run id and commit; (2) the serving start-up reads the digest for the approved alias from the registry; (3) it downloads to a private path, calls verify_artifact, and only then loads; (4) a mismatch aborts start-up and raises an alert instead of falling back to 'newest file'. The executed test confirms a file with one appended byte is rejected, and that an uppercase hex digest is accepted after normalisation.

concise_answer: Hashing a user ID does not anonymise it: an unsalted hash of a guessable ID can be recomputed, and pseudonymised data is often still personal data (jurisdiction and counsel decide). Minimise what is logged (coarsen date of birth and postcode, drop unused fields, sample), use a keyed pseudonym held separately, set retention by purpose (about the 90-day label window plus slack), audit access, and keep a way to find a person's rows for access and deletion requests where they apply.
detailed_answer:
Problems in the current design. (1) Unsalted hashing of an identifier with a small or structured space (emails, phone numbers, sequential IDs) can be reversed by hashing candidates, and any party who already has the raw IDs can join to it. Pseudonymisation lowers risk but pseudonymised data is generally still treated as personal data, because re-identification remains possible with additional information (the UK ICO's guidance says it is personal data in the hands of anyone who holds the additional information, which includes the team holding the key and the raw IDs); exactly where the line sits for a given recipient depends on jurisdiction and legal advice. (2) Date of birth plus postcode is a classic quasi-identifier combination (Sweeney estimated, from 1990 US census data, that about 87% of the US population was likely unique on 5-digit ZIP, gender and date of birth), so even without the ID some rows may be re-identifiable. (3) Indefinite retention keeps risk long after the purpose ended. (4) Logging every feature of every request is more than monitoring usually needs.

Engineering changes. Minimise at the source: log only features the model actually uses, store age band or year instead of full date of birth, and a coarse postcode region if the model tolerates it. Sample: logging a fraction of requests is often enough for skew and drift checks, and the Rules of Machine Learning note that saving serving-time features for even a small fraction of examples is useful. Replace the hash with a keyed pseudonym (an HMAC whose secret sits in a key manager, separate from the warehouse; rotating it changes every pseudonym, so plan a re-keying job or accept broken linkage with older rows), so linking requires access to the key. Define retention by purpose: row-level logs must live long enough to join with labels (here about 90 days plus a buffer for late labels and retraining windows), then are deleted or reduced to aggregates; training snapshots derived from them get their own retention. Control access with roles, and audit queries on the table. Keep a lookup that can find a person's rows (the keyed pseudonym allows this) so deletion and access requests can be honoured where they apply (the right to erasure is not absolute; what applies depends on jurisdiction and legal advice), and ensure derived tables are covered by lineage.

Destroying the key later may make rows hard to link, but whether the remaining columns are then anonymous depends on how re-identifiable they are; do not claim anonymisation on that basis alone without review.

answer:
Delete everywhere the data can be located, and promise only what the system can actually demonstrate.

What is deletable: the source records, the offline and online feature-store entries, prediction and feature logs, caches, analysts' exports, and stored training snapshots. This only works if there is lineage: an index from a person (via a keyed pseudonym or ID) to every dataset, snapshot and export that contains them. Without it you can only guess. Backups should have a bounded expiry so deleted data ages out of them.

Trained models are different. For most model types there is no general, exact operation that removes one person's influence from the weights short of retraining without them. Approximate unlearning methods exist, but they are model-dependent, research-grade, and not something to promise as equivalent to retraining. So the honest statements are: the data was removed from the stores listed by a stated date; the next scheduled retraining (the nightly one from the first run that reads the tombstone list, the others at their next cycle) will not include it; older model versions are retired according to a stated retention policy. Whether residual influence in an already-trained model is acceptable, or whether an out-of-cycle retrain is required, depends on jurisdiction and legal counsel. Do not claim that the model 'forgot' the person.

Design to make this cheap: keep a deletion/tombstone list that every training job applies at read time, so deleted IDs cannot re-enter from an old extract; make training reproducible from versioned data so a retrain without specific rows is a routine job; keep retrain cadence and model retention short enough to state a bounded time; record dataset versions in the registry so you can list which model versions saw the data; avoid copying raw personal data into places lineage does not reach. Models can retain recognisable traces of individual records (the Secret Sharer study found unintended memorisation of rare sequences in language models, arising early in training rather than only from overtraining, and, in its appendix experiments, increasing with model size and batch size), so treat that as a factor in how aggressively you retrain; this is model- and data-dependent and absence of memorisation is hard to demonstrate.

concise_answer: A model card is a short document that accompanies a trained model and records its intended use, how it was evaluated, and its performance across relevant conditions or groups. For a credit model, require: intended and out-of-scope uses, training and evaluation data description, metrics overall and by slice, limitations and known failure modes, owner and version, and a link to the lineage record. Generate the metric sections from the evaluation run.
detailed_answer:
A model card, as introduced in the 'Model Cards for Model Reporting' paper, is a short document accompanying a trained model. The paper describes it as reporting benchmarked evaluation across different conditions (including demographic and other groups where relevant), the context the model is intended for, and details of how the evaluation was done, so that users can see where the model is and is not suitable.

As a release artifact, treat it like a changelog or test report: it is versioned with the model, produced by the pipeline, and checked by the promotion gate rather than written once after launch. For a credit-scoring model, a gate might require these fields:

- Model details: owner, version, training date, model type, link to the registry entry, code commit and data version (lineage).
- Intended use and out-of-scope use: for example, scoring existing customers for limit changes but not for automated final decisions on a new product.
- Data: training and evaluation sources, time ranges, known gaps, label definition and delay.
- Metrics: overall and per slice (for example age band, region, new vs existing customers), with sample sizes and uncertainty, plus the decision threshold and calibration.
- Limitations and failure modes: populations or conditions with weak performance, sensitivity to missing features, known drift sensitivities.
- Ethical and fairness considerations: sensitive attributes used or excluded, subgroup error-rate gaps, and the sign-off decision on them.
- Monitoring and rollback: what is tracked in production and who is on call.
- Review and approval: who signed off and when.

Keeping the card trustworthy: auto-fill the numbers from the evaluation job so they cannot drift from reality, and block promotion if required sections are empty or older than the model. A card does not make a model fair or safe; it makes claims inspectable. Which fields regulators or auditors require depends on jurisdiction, and that is a question for compliance rather than something this template settles.

concise_answer: This is membership inference: models often behave differently on records they were trained on, for example with higher confidence or lower loss, so an attacker who can query can sometimes guess membership. It is worse with overfitting, small data or rare records. Cheap mitigations: reduce overfitting (targets the root signal); return less or round scores (label-only attacks still work); authenticate and rate-limit (does not stop a single-query test; keys can be multiplied). Strongest but costlier: differentially private training.
detailed_answer:
The risk. A model is usually more confident, or has lower loss, on examples it was trained on than on similar unseen ones. An attacker who can query the model with a person's record, and who has some idea of how members and non-members score, can sometimes decide whether the record was a member. Membership alone can be sensitive (being in a medical-condition dataset reveals something). It tends to be worse when the model overfits (a large gap between training and held-out performance), when the training set is small, when records are rare or outliers, and when the API exposes rich outputs such as full probability vectors at high precision. Model inversion (reconstructing attributes or inputs from outputs) is a related but different risk.

Mitigations by what they achieve:
- Reduce the generalisation gap (regularisation, early stopping, more data). Addresses the root signal for many attacks; OWASP's membership-inference page lists regularisation among its prevention methods.
- Return less: the label or a coarse bucket instead of the full vector, and rounding scores. These remove fine-grained signal but label-only attacks exist and defeat defences that only mask confidence scores (Choquette-Choo et al.), so they should not be relied on as a defence on their own.
- Authentication, per-key quotas and rate limits. These raise the cost of attacks that need many queries (for example label-only attacks, which probe each record with a few augmented queries up to thousands for boundary-distance attacks) but do nothing against a single-query threshold test by an authorised caller (at 10,000 calls a day one key could test up to 10,000 records, about 3,300 if each needs three augmented queries, but only about 4 at the 2,500 queries of the paper's boundary-distance attack), and per-key limits can be sidestepped with many keys (the paper notes Sybil attacks make query limiting an unlikely defence).
- Monitoring unusual query patterns (many near-duplicate records from one key). Detects some probing; not prevention.
- Differentially private training. (OWASP also lists adding noise to predictions, but noise on scores that leaves the label unchanged is a form of confidence masking and does not stop label-only attacks.) DP training gives a formal bound on how much any one record can influence the model, at a cost in accuracy, complexity and compute; Choquette-Choo et al. report DP and strong L2 regularisation as the only known defences that stopped their label-only attacks (at an accuracy cost; DP's epsilon was large at useful accuracy). It is the strongest option but not cheap.

No single cheap control closes the risk; choose a combination matched to how sensitive membership is.
practical_answer:
Measure before you spend. A one-sprint check you can run on your own model:

1. Hold out a set of records that were never in training (non-members), drawn from the same distribution as the training data (a random split, not a later period, or drift will inflate the AUC), and sample an equal number of training records (members).
2. Query the production scoring path and record, for each record, a simple signal: the model's loss on the true label, or the maximum predicted probability.
3. Compute the AUC of that signal for separating members from non-members. An AUC close to 0.5 means this simple attack learns little; values clearly above 0.5, for example 0.6 or higher, mean the model separates members and you should act. (The cut-off is a judgement, not a standard.)
4. Repeat after each mitigation (stronger regularisation, rounding to 2 decimals, label-only output) and record the accuracy cost next to the AUC, so the decision is a trade-off table.
5. Re-run the test whenever the model type, training set size or output format changes; add it to the release checklist next to the model card.

This tests only the simplest attack; a low AUC is not a proof of safety, only evidence that cheap attacks fail. Also report the true-positive rate at a low false-positive rate (for example 0.1%, which needs at least several thousand non-members to estimate), since a near-0.5 AUC can hide a handful of confidently identified records.

detailed_answer:
Start by deciding whether to mitigate first. If p99 is breaching the SLO and burning budget quickly, shifting most traffic back to v11 buys time for the investigation (keep a small slice or a replay on v12 so versions can still be compared); diagnose from the captured data rather than live-debugging customers.

The pattern is the clue: the median barely moved (+3 ms) while the tail more than tripled, and the unchanged error rate suggests the slow requests still finish inside client timeouts (check retry counts, because retries can hide a failing tail). That points away from 'the model is uniformly slower' (which would shift the whole distribution) and towards something that hits a subset of requests or creates queueing under certain conditions. Work in this order.

1. Scope it. Split latency by model version, replica, request size or shape, time since replica start, and hour. If only young replicas are slow, suspect warm-up (lazy initialisation, compilation on first use of each input shape). If only large inputs are slow, suspect input-dependent cost.
2. Saturation. Check CPU throttling against the container limit (a new model using more threads than the CPU limit allows can be throttled in bursts), queue depth, and memory pressure. Rising queues with unchanged mean service time show up in the tail first.
3. Batching and concurrency settings. A larger max batch or wait timeout added for throughput adds waiting time for the unlucky requests.
4. Added dependencies. A new feature or lookup in v12's path means another remote call whose own p99 now adds to yours.
5. Garbage collection or allocator pauses from a bigger model or larger intermediate objects.
6. Serialisation and payload size of the response.

Why the offline benchmark missed it: it likely measured single-request, warm, average inputs without production concurrency, tail-sized inputs, dependency latency, or cold replicas. Reproduce by replaying logged production requests against v12 at production concurrency. Report percentiles by version, not averages; and compare to the last week's same hour to exclude traffic-mix effects.
practical_answer:
A triage table you can use as a runbook; the 'quick test' column should take minutes with existing dashboards or a replay:

| Observation | Likely cause | Quick test |
|---|---|---|
| Slow only in the first minutes after a replica starts | Warm-up / lazy init | Slice latency by replica age; send synthetic warm-up requests before readiness |
| Slow only for large or unusual inputs | Input-dependent cost, per-shape recompilation | Bucket latency by payload size; replay the worst 1% of logged requests |
| Periodic spikes at fixed intervals | CPU throttling, GC | Compare throttled-time counters and GC logs with spike times |
| p99 tracks batch size or queue wait | Batching timeout too long | Lower max wait on one canary replica and re-measure |
| p99 rises with a dependency's p99 | New remote call in the path | Trace spans per call; test with the call stubbed |

Decision rule: if no cause is found within the agreed time-box (say 30 minutes) while the SLO is burning, keep traffic on v11 and continue offline with a replay, rather than leaving the regression live.

detailed_answer:
First hour: mitigate, then diagnose. If the previous image and its lockfile are known good, roll back the whole environment (image, libraries and model together) rather than patching forward. If you cannot roll back, add an output guard that treats a non-finite or out-of-range score as a failure and routes to a fallback decision (for example send to manual review), and flag those responses so they are counted. Keep the bad build and a sample of the affected inputs for analysis.

Finding the cause is a differential problem: the same inputs go through an old and a new environment, and you find the first stage where results diverge.

1. Take a few thousand logged requests (including some that produced NaN) and run them in both environments.
2. Compare stage by stage: raw inputs, parsed features, preprocessed features, model output. The earliest differing stage identifies the layer.
3. Typical mechanisms. A library changed a default or its handling of missing values, categories or dtypes, so features collapse to defaults (which can also explain the narrow score range). Columns are matched by position in one version and by name in another, so a reordered column shifts every feature. A scaler divides by a zero standard deviation for a constant column, or log of zero appears after a changed clipping default. Lower-precision arithmetic overflows. A serialized model loaded under a different library version warns but runs with changed behaviour.
4. Confirm by pinning one suspect library at a time in the new image.

Prevention: lock files that pin transitive dependencies with hashes; dependency upgrades treated as releases that go through CI with a golden-input regression test (fixed inputs, expected outputs within a tolerance chosen from measured run-to-run noise) and a canary; a serving-time sanity check that scores are finite and within range; and an alert on NaN rate. The ML Test Score rubric lists explicitly monitoring the first occurrence of NaNs or infinities, and practising rollback of serving models, as items.
practical_answer:
A concrete golden-input regression spec that would have caught this in CI (all numbers are examples to adapt):

- Fixture: 2,000 anonymised or synthetic requests that cover every feature type, each category plus an unseen category, missing values, zeros, and the largest and smallest values seen in production; stored with the outputs of the currently deployed build.
- Checks on the candidate build: (1) every score is finite; (2) every score lies in the valid range (0 to 1 for a probability); (3) the maximum absolute difference from the stored outputs is below a tolerance you derive by running the current build twice on different hardware (if run-to-run noise is about 1e-6, a tolerance near 1e-4 would flag real changes without flaking); (4) the fraction of rows whose score changes by more than 0.01 is below an agreed small bound, for example 0.1%; (5) the score standard deviation is within a band around the stored value, which catches 'narrowing'.
- Runtime guard: reject non-finite outputs, count them as a labelled metric, and page if more than, say, 0.1% of a 5-minute window is affected.
- Release rule: any dependency change forces the fixture run plus a canary at a small traffic share before full rollout.

Review changes to the tolerances as deliberately as code changes, since loosening them is how regressions get through.

detailed_answer:
Quantify first. Growth from 0.9 GiB to the 2 GiB limit in about 11 hours is 1.1 GiB / 11 h, or about 0.1 GiB (roughly 102 MiB) per hour. At 10 requests/s that is 36,000 requests per hour, so about 2.9 KiB of memory per request if growth is proportional to requests (at flat traffic growth per hour and per request look identical, so confirm with the traffic test below). A small, constant amount per request suggests a per-request object that is never released, not a one-off large allocation.

Separate three behaviours.
- True leak: memory grows without bound in proportion to requests and does not level off. Check whether the slope follows traffic (halve the traffic in staging; the slope should roughly halve) and whether memory stays high when traffic stops (a leak and allocator retention both do, so use the live-object comparison below to tell them apart).
- Bounded cache: growth levels off once the cache reaches its size limit or the set of distinct keys is exhausted. A cache with no size bound keyed by something near-unique per request (request ID, raw feature tuple, timestamp) behaves like a leak until it fills the node.
- Fragmentation or allocator retention: resident memory stays high while the live-object size reported inside the runtime is flat. It is usually bounded, so resident size tends to plateau high rather than climb linearly without end; a steady linear climb at flat traffic fits a leak or an unbounded cache better.

Finding the source. Compare the runtime's live-object accounting with the process's resident size; if the first is flat but the second climbs, suspect native memory, the allocator, or buffers held by a native library. If the first grows, take two heap snapshots a few hours apart under replayed production traffic and diff them by allocation site (in Python, the standard library's tracemalloc supports snapshot comparison). Common culprits in model services: an unbounded dict or list keeping per-request results, exceptions or tracebacks stored in a list, metrics labels with unbounded cardinality, request tracing buffers, and, in PyTorch services, stored output tensors that still carry autograd history because inference ran with gradient tracking on.

Keep it healthy meanwhile: compute projected time to OOM (limit minus current, divided by slope) and alert well before it; recycle workers after a fixed number of requests with a graceful drain so restarts are not abrupt; verify the fix with the same replay and a flat slope over at least a couple of times the old time-to-OOM. Raising the limit only delays the failure.
practical_answer:
Worked procedure with the numbers from this case:

1. Baseline: 0.9 GiB at start; slope about 0.1 GiB/hour; limit 2 GiB, so about 11 hours to failure. Alert when projected time-to-OOM drops below, say, 3 hours (at about 1.7 GiB).
2. Reproduce in staging with replayed traffic at 10 requests/s. If the slope does not appear, the trigger is a rare input class or a dependency path; replay the full distribution including errors.
3. Experiment ladder, one change at a time, 2 hours each: disable the prediction cache; disable request tracing; disable the feature-logging buffer; run inference with gradient tracking off. The step that flattens the slope identifies the owner.
4. Verify per-request cost: after the fix the slope should be near 0 over 24 hours; if it drops from about 2.9 KiB/request to, say, 0.1 KiB/request, check that residual too.
5. Interim guard: recycle each worker after about 200,000 requests (about 5.5 hours at this load if one worker took all traffic; scale the number to your worker count), drain connections before restart, and stagger workers so they never restart together.
6. Postmortem item: add the memory slope to the release checklist so a model update is soaked for at least a few multiples of the typical restart interval before full rollout.

detailed_answer:
Default to the mitigation that is fastest, best understood and most reversible, and keep the two options from being treated as a pure choice: shifting traffic weight back to the old bundle, or turning the new feature off with a flag, is often faster than redeploying either build.

Decision inputs.
1. Cost of waiting. Current harm per minute (4% fewer approvals) against the error budget or business tolerance. If harm is high, mitigate now and diagnose later.
2. Is the rollback target good? Rollback is only safe if the whole previous bundle still works: old model, old preprocessing, and the features it expects. If the new feature pipeline replaced or dropped inputs the old model needs (the question notes that the new feature has been written for 30 minutes, so check whether the old model can still read those rows), rolling back the model alone may produce a different failure. The ML Test Score rubric lists 'Models can be quickly and safely rolled back to a previous serving version' as a test and says rollback should be practised outside emergencies, so rehearsed, not assumed.
3. Confidence in the diagnosis. A one-line fix for a bug you have not proven to be the whole cause is a hypothesis; rolling forward then risks 25 minutes of waiting and a second regression. If the model itself is also flawed, the fix will not restore the metric.
4. Time to effect and verification path. Roll-forward needs CI, deploy and bake time; rollback may be a single alias or traffic-weight change.
5. Shared causes. If the old model also depends on the broken data source, rollback will not help.

Reasonable policy: if the rollback bundle is tested, restore it (or shift most traffic to it) first, because it is quick and reversible; roll forward when rollback is itself unsafe, when the cause is proven and the fix verified in a pre-production replay, or when the fault is in shared infrastructure.

First five minutes: freeze further deployments, name an incident lead, shift the new model's traffic share down using the control you already have, disable the new feature with a flag if one exists (so the feature takes its default, which is safe only if the model was trained to handle that default), record the timeline, quarantine or mark the feature values written in the last 30 minutes so they are not served or reused for training, and confirm recovery against a concurrent control if one exists, otherwise against the same hour a week earlier, not a feeling.

A simple scoring grid to use when choosing, with example values for this incident (adapt weights to your own risk appetite):

| Question | Rollback | Roll-forward |
|---|---|---|
| Time to take effect | about 5 min if the bundle was rehearsed | about 25 min plus bake time |
| Evidence that the action fixes it | high: the previous bundle produced the earlier metric | medium: only the feature bug is proven, the model may also be at fault |
| Risk the action causes a new failure | depends on whether old model and the 30 minutes of new-feature data coexist; replay a sample of recent requests through the old bundle in 2 minutes to find out | a one-line change in a rushed pipeline |
| Reversible? | yes, if both bundles stay deployable | partly |

Decision rule: while you freeze deployments and start shifting a small share of traffic to the old bundle, run the 2-minute replay of recent requests through it. If outputs look normal, roll back fully; if they are broken (missing or defaulted inputs), restore the old feature path or a safe default first and then roll back; if that cannot be done within minutes, roll forward with the fix behind a feature flag in a small canary first. Whichever path is taken, hold a short postmortem; a rollback or traffic reroute by the on-call is, in the SRE Book's list, a typical postmortem trigger.
