detailed_answer:
At 99.95% over 30 days the error budget is only 0.0005 x 43,200 = 21.6 minutes, so last month's 22-minute feature-store outage, if every request failed throughout, used essentially all of it (a 31-day month allows 22.3 minutes). The two dependencies have different roles, so they need different designs.

Registry (start-up dependency). It should not be reachable from the request path or needed to scale. Make replicas self-sufficient: bake the approved model into the image, or have start-up read from a node-local or regional read-through cache keyed by the pinned artifact digest, so a registry outage only blocks promotion of new versions, not scaling. If the registry is down, start from the last known good verified artifact rather than failing, and refuse to start from an unverified one. Keep a minimum number of warm replicas as headroom so autoscaling is not the only source of capacity.

Feature store (request-path dependency). Define a ladder of degraded modes, each with a rule for when it applies:
1. Normal.
2. Stale cache: per-process or shared cache of recent feature values, usable if within a staleness bound derived from how quickly each feature changes (a rarely changing tenure may be hours old; a velocity counter may be minutes).
3. Request-only model: a smaller model trained and validated on features available in the request itself, so its behaviour under missing features is known.
4. Safe default: a business-defined action (route to review, show popular items), not an arbitrary constant.
Protect the path with short timeouts well under the client's budget, circuit breakers so a failing store is not hammered, and bounded retries with jitter. On recovery, close the circuit gradually and confirm that feature writes missed during the outage are backfilled (or the features are fresh again) before leaving the fallback modes.

Two pitfalls. Defaults filled in at serving must match how training treated missing values, or the fallback itself becomes skew. And degraded code paths rarely run, so they are likely broken when needed; the SRE Book makes this point about graceful degradation and recommends exercising it regularly.

Observability and data hygiene: tag every prediction with the mode that produced it; count fallback rate as its own SLI (a valid, in-time fallback response normally counts as good for the availability SLO, which is why the fallback rate needs its own objective; decide this in advance); and exclude or mark degraded predictions when building training and evaluation sets so retraining does not learn from them as normal.
practical_answer:
Example degradation table with example numbers (adapt to your latency budget and features):

| Mode | Trigger | Behaviour | Max duration without paging |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 normal | store p99 below 20 ms, error rate below 1% | live features | n/a |
| 2 stale cache | 5 consecutive failures or 50% errors in 10 s (circuit opens) | cached features no older than 15 min; a miss or older entry sends that request to mode 3 | about 15 min (then entries have aged out) |
| 3 request-only model | cache miss or stale beyond 15 min | fallback model on request-only features | 30 min |
| 4 safe default | fallback model unhealthy | business default action | page immediately |

Registry drill: block registry access from a staging cluster, then scale a deployment from 2 to 10 replicas; all new replicas must start from the cached verified artifact within the normal start-up time, and a replica given a file with a wrong digest must refuse to start.

Game-day test: inject 100% errors on the feature store for 30 minutes at production-like load; pass criteria are that availability SLI stays within budget, the circuit opens within seconds, requests are labelled by mode, and recovery back to mode 1 happens without a thundering herd (re-close the circuit gradually).

detailed_answer:
Availability and latency SLIs describe whether the service answered, not whether the answer was good, so a model service needs SLIs on the quality of what it returns. The SRE material frames the error budget as the allowed unreliability that decides whether releases continue; the same mechanism works for quality if quality is turned into countable good and bad events.

Fast proxy SLIs (available in minutes, no labels). Define a prediction as 'good' when its inputs were fresh (each critical feature updated within its allowed age), not defaulted or imputed, within the training range, and produced by the intended model. Add distribution checks: input drift against a reference window and the shape of the score distribution. Compare agreement with a shadow or previous model on live traffic. These detect events like the nine-day stale feature early. They are proxies, so calibrate thresholds from historical variation and treat them as leading indicators.

Slow ground-truth SLIs. When labels mature, compute accuracy or calibration on cohorts by prediction date and set an SLO on them (for example, the share of weekly cohorts above a quality floor). Because of the three-week delay, this budget is accounted retroactively: it confirms or corrects the proxy signals and tunes the proxy thresholds.

SLOs and alerts. Choose targets such as 'at least 99% of predictions in a 28-day window are fresh and non-defaulted', and alert on burn rate over short and long windows, as with availability.

Policy text. The SRE Workbook's example policy halts changes and releases other than P0 issues or security fixes until the service is back within its SLO, lists explicit exemptions (for example outages caused by something outside the service's control), and requires a postmortem when a single incident consumes more than a set share of the budget. Adapt that to quality: let the proxy budget drive the immediate freeze and paging, and the matured-label budget confirm, extend or lift it; when the proxy quality budget is exhausted, freeze non-urgent model and feature releases (fixes to the data or the monitoring itself are exempt), prioritise freshness checks, data contracts and monitoring, and require a postmortem for large single burns. Be explicit about which team is accountable for upstream data. Do not let proxies replace ground truth; review them against matured labels each quarter.

Impact. Silent failures need counterfactual estimates. Use logged predictions and outcomes: compare CTR in the 19-day window to the pre-rename baseline (the preceding weeks, matched by weekday and adjusted for seasonality; a window shifted by only a week would overlap the incident), or, if one existed, to a holdout slice still served with the old feature (a shadow model has no click outcomes; it can only show how scores and rankings would have differed on logged requests). State the estimated lost clicks or revenue as a range with method, not a single confident number. Also state the exposure: how many users and requests were affected, and whether some segments (for example, users who relied most on that feature) were hit harder.

Why detection was slow. List contributing factors, not a culprit. Likely ones: the monitoring watched service health (errors, latency) and the pipeline ran green; no check on feature default or null rates; no data contract with the upstream team, so a rename was not a breaking change; quality was reviewed weekly from a business metric with natural noise, and a gradual ramp (a 7% relative loss) is easy to miss; a loss that ramps over 19 days when the default applied to every user needs its own explanation (for example cached recommendations or daily-refreshed features ageing out, or a staged rollout of the rename), which the postmortem should check rather than assume. The Rules of Machine Learning describe this class of failure, for example a joined table that is no longer updated, which degrades quality slowly without errors.

Blameless format. The SRE Book's postmortem guidance is that a blameless postmortem assumes everyone involved had good intentions and focuses on fixing systems and processes. It also lists a monitoring failure, which usually means manual discovery, as a trigger for a postmortem; this incident qualifies.

Action items (owners and dates): data contract tests on upstream schemas; an alert on per-feature default and null rate (a jump from near 0% to 100% is unambiguous); freshness checks; a comparison of live feature values and scores against a logged reference (the training distribution or a frozen sample of earlier requests), since a canary against the previous model shares the same broken upstream data; a daily business-metric guardrail with a threshold on trend not just level; a reprocessing plan if training data collected in the window was affected.

Avoid: naming the upstream engineer as root cause, an action list of 'be more careful', a single unsourced revenue number, and closing without verifying the new alert fires in a test.
practical_answer:
Runbook for a silent quality alert (first 60 minutes):

1. Confirm with an independent signal: another metric, or the same metric by segment; rule out a tracking or logging change.
2. List changes in the last 30 days: model, feature definitions, upstream schemas, traffic mix, experiments.
3. Check per-feature default, null and freshness rates for the window; a feature at 100% default is the first thing to rule out.
4. Replay a sample of logged requests through the previous model or feature version and compare scores.
5. Mitigate: restore the renamed column or add a mapping (a model rollback helps only if the older model does not read it), disable the feature only if the model was trained or validated with it missing (otherwise this reproduces the fault), in which case it is intentionally imputed and flagged, or switch to the fallback model; record the exact time.
6. Estimate impact from logs (affected requests, segments) and snapshot the evidence before it ages out.
7. Communicate: what is known, what is not, next update time.
8. Open the postmortem within a few days; fix the detection gap as well as the root cause, because the detection gap is what turned a column rename into a 19-day loss.

Timeline template: first bad request; first alert that could have fired; detection; mitigation; full recovery. The 19-day gap between the first bad request and detection is the main finding, so measure each interval and state a target for time to detect.

import math


def daily_cost(hourly_rps, rps_per_replica, target_util, cost_per_replica_hour,
               min_replicas=2, cache_hit=0.0, static_replicas=None):
    """Return (cost, requests, cost_per_1k_requests) for one day.

    hourly_rps: 24 average request rates. A cache hit removes that share of requests from the model tier.
    static_replicas: if set, that many replicas run all day; otherwise replicas follow load each hour.
    """
    requests = sum(r * 3600 for r in hourly_rps)
    cost = 0.0
    for r in hourly_rps:
        model_rps = r * (1.0 - cache_hit)
        if static_replicas is not None:
            n = static_replicas
        else:
            n = max(min_replicas, math.ceil(model_rps / (rps_per_replica * target_util)))
        cost += n * cost_per_replica_hour
    return cost, requests, 1000.0 * cost / requests

answer:
Match the capacity type to how each workload tolerates interruption and cold starts.

(1) Nightly fine-tune: a good fit for reclaimable capacity, provided the job is resumable. Checkpoint model, optimizer and data-loader state and RNG at a fixed interval, and let the orchestrator restart on interruption. With a checkpoint every 15 minutes, each interruption costs at most about 15 minutes of repeated work plus restore time; two interruptions with 5-minute restores bound the extra at roughly 40 minutes on a 7-hour job (about 10%) in this example, provided replacement capacity arrives within the restore time. Set a deadline rule: if interruptions exceed a threshold or the job risks missing its morning deadline, fall back to standard capacity. Check that checkpoints are written to durable storage, not local disk, and that checkpoint write time is small relative to the checkpoint interval. Change my mind if interruptions are frequent enough that wasted work erases the discount, or if the job is not resumable.

(2) Internal classifier: scale-to-zero looks attractive for 200 requests a day, but the first request each morning waits about 3 minutes. Options: scale to zero overnight and run a scheduled warm-up shortly before the workday; keep one replica from, say, 07:45 to 18:00 on weekdays (about 10 hours instead of 24); or make the interface asynchronous. Pick by how bad a 3-minute wait is for staff versus idle spend. Reducing cold start (smaller model, cached weights on the node) shifts the answer towards pure scale-to-zero.

(3) Customer-facing endpoint: keep a baseline of on-demand replicas sized for steady load with headroom, because reclamation can remove many replicas at once and notice is short. Reclaimable capacity can be used for burst replicas above the baseline, spread across zones and instance types, with graceful draining, as long as the SLO holds if all of it disappears. Autoscaling should use a signal that reflects accelerator load such as queue depth or concurrent requests. Change my mind if traffic is highly spiky and reclamation is rare in your environment, or if a degraded fallback is acceptable.

question: Your ticket-triage service calls a hosted LLM through a model name that the provider re-points to its newest release. One Monday the share of tickets routed to 'billing' drops from 31% to 22% and the thumbs-down rate rises, although you deployed no code and no prompt change. Design the release process so that a provider-side model change is handled like any other dependency upgrade: what you pin and record, what you test before switching, how you roll out, and what you do when the provider announces a retirement date for the model you use.
answer:
Stop treating the model identifier as a constant: in production, reference a specific dated snapshot where the provider offers one (not an alias that is re-pointed), and treat the tuple (model id, prompt version, decoding parameters, tool/JSON schemas, any guardrail versions) as one release unit that is logged on every request. The Monday drop is then diagnosable: you can see from the model identifier recorded on each request (the resolved snapshot returned in the response, where the API reports it) whether the underlying model changed, and rolling back is a configuration change back to the previous pin (provided the provider still serves it).

Before switching to a new model, run the same prompt on a golden set, ideally including replayed, de-identified production tickets with human-confirmed routes, and compare per route, not only overall: a 9-point drop in one class can be invisible in an overall accuracy number. Also compare format validity, refusal rate, tokens per request and latency, because a newer model may be more verbose or slower.

Then roll out like any model: mirror or shadow a slice of live traffic, canary by user hash at a small percentage with the routing distribution, schema-validity rate and feedback as guardrails, and keep the old pin ready for instant rollback. The ML Test Score treats dependency changes (it lists notification on dependency changes) and canarying models before production serving as tests a production ML system should have; a hosted model is a dependency you do not control.

For retirement notices: keep a calendar of every pinned model and its announced end date, start the migration with enough lead time to run the full gate and a canary, and keep a tested fallback model in config. Pitfalls: even a pinned snapshot may be retired, and provider-side serving changes can in some setups alter behaviour slightly, so keep a scheduled replay of the golden set (for example daily) as a drift alarm. Check what stability the provider actually documents rather than assuming it.
common_mistakes: Treating the model name as a constant and only versioning the prompt text
Judging the new model on the overall pass rate alone, so a routing shift in one class stays hidden
Assuming a pinned snapshot is permanent and never planning for retirement
interview_style_note: Treats a hosted model as a versioned dependency whose change needs the same gates as code: pin, replay, canary, rollback, and a migration calendar.

topic: LLMOps specifics (prompt versioning, eval gates, token cost, guardrail monitoring)
question: Your assistant has an input filter and a separate output-moderation classifier, and the dashboard shows one number, 'blocked responses'. After Tuesday's release it goes from 1.2% to 3.9% of requests and p95 latency is also up 15%. No one has filed an incident. How do you decide whether this is real harmful traffic, a prompt or model change, or a mis-calibrated guardrail, and what must already be logged so that this is a 30-minute job rather than a 3-day one?
concise_answer: Segment the jump by guardrail, reason code, prompt/model version, tenant and release time: a step change at the deploy implicates your change, gradual or single-tenant growth implicates traffic. Sample 50-100 blocked items for human review and replay them on the previous versions; check whether block-and-regenerate loops explain the latency. Log request id, resolved prompt version, model id, guardrail version, score, action and stage timings, and alert on a falling block rate too (fail-open).
detailed_answer:
Start from the dashboard, not the model. The headline 'blocked responses' mixes several things, so break the 1.2% to 3.9% jump down by guardrail (input filter vs output moderation), reason code or category, prompt version and model id, tenant, route and language, and time relative to the release. The pattern points to the cause: a step change exactly at the deploy implicates your change (prompt, model, classifier version or threshold) unless an external event, such as a campaign or a new customer, landed the same day; a gradual rise or a single-tenant concentration implicates traffic; a rise in one category most often means either a real abuse campaign or a classifier that over-triggers on a new input pattern (or the release changed what the model outputs in that category).

The latency increase is a clue. If the system regenerates or retries when the output moderator blocks, a higher block rate creates extra model calls and raises p95 by itself, so the two symptoms may share one cause. Compare per-stage timings with the block-and-retry count, and check whether the release itself added a guardrail call, a longer prompt or a slower model.

Then sample. Pull 50 to 100 blocked items across categories (with that few labels the estimated false-positive share is rough, about plus or minus 10 to 14 points at 95% confidence for a share near 50%; label more for a tighter estimate), have a reviewer label each as correctly blocked or false positive, and replay the same inputs through the previous prompt, model and guardrail versions offline. Labelling especially the newly blocked items (those the previous versions would have passed) yields the share of the 2.7 extra points that is genuine policy-violating traffic versus over-blocking, and the replay shows which component changed behaviour.

What to log so this takes 30 minutes: request id, tenant, the resolved prompt version number (not only an alias: an alias is a mutable pointer, while prompt versions in MLflow's prompt registry are immutable), model id, guardrail name and version, score and threshold, action taken (block, regenerate, redact, pass), and per-stage timings.

Alert in both directions. A sudden fall in block rate can mean the guardrail is failing open (for example timeouts treated as pass), which can be the more dangerous failure because harmful content then passes unnoticed. Pitfalls: alerting only on a global rate, and tuning the threshold until the graph looks normal before establishing which blocked cases are false positives.
common_mistakes: Alerting on one global block rate and tuning the threshold until the graph looks normal
Assuming every blocked request is a genuine policy violation
Logging only the prompt alias, so the served version cannot be reconstructed
interview_style_note: Segments the metric, uses release timing and sampled human review to attribute the cause, and asks for the logging that makes attribution cheap.

question: A multi-tenant support assistant handles 300,000 requests/day. Each call sends about 2,400 tokens of fixed content (system prompt, policy text, tool definitions) plus about 800 variable tokens and produces about 350 output tokens. Finance reports that the LLM bill grew 40% in a month while traffic grew 8%, and one tenant looks responsible. Using relative units (1k input tokens = 1 unit, 1k output tokens = 4 units, hypothetical), compute the baseline cost per request, estimate the saving from an 80% prefix-cache hit rate (cached input at 0.5 units/1k) and from routing half the traffic to a smaller model at 0.25x cost, and describe the attribution, budget and alerting controls plus the release checks that stop quality loss.
concise_answer: Baseline is (2.4+0.8) x 1 + 0.35 x 4 = 4.6 units per request. With an 80% hit rate on the fixed prefix at 0.5 units/1k it is 3.64 (-21%); routing half the traffic to a 0.25x model on top gives 2.275 (-51%). At fixed prices, cost per request rose about 30% (1.40/1.08), likely from more tokens, retries or model mix, so attribute usage per tenant, set budgets and alerts, and gate routing with per-slice evals and a canary.
detailed_answer:
Baseline arithmetic (relative units, hypothetical ratios): input 3.2k tokens x 1 unit/1k = 3.2, output 0.35k x 4 = 1.4, so 4.6 units per request and 1.38 million units/day at 300,000 requests.

Why did the bill grow 40% on 8% more traffic? Cost scales with total tokens (requests times tokens per request), so 8% more requests cannot explain a 40% rise: cost per request must have risen by about 30% at unchanged prices (1.40 / 1.08 = 1.30). Typical culprits are one tenant sending much longer variable context (pasting whole email threads), a longer system prompt or more tool definitions after a release, more tool-call rounds or retries, and more verbose outputs. Concretely, if one tenant's variable input goes from 800 to 2,400 tokens, its per-request cost goes from 4.6 to 6.2 units (+35%). That explains the 30% rise only if the tenant is about 85% of the traffic (0.30 / 0.35): at a 20% share the blended cost per request rises by just 7% (0.8 x 4.6 + 0.2 x 6.2 = 4.92), so check the other drivers too. You can only see this if every call is attributed to a tenant, feature and prompt version.

Prefix caching: cache reuse typically requires the beginning of the prompt to match exactly (OpenAI's documentation says the entire rendered prefix must match), so put the 2,400 fixed tokens first and per-request material last, and keep timestamps and user ids out of the prefix. If, hypothetically, 80% of requests hit a cache that charges 0.5 units/1k for cached input, the fixed part costs 2.4 x (0.8 x 0.5 + 0.2 x 1) = 1.44 instead of 2.4, so a request costs 3.64 units (-21%). Cache behaviour, discounts and retention are provider-specific and change, so read the provider's documentation (including any cache-write surcharge, which this arithmetic ignores) and measure the cached-token counts it reports. Note that an edit to the fixed prefix (system prompt, policy text, tool definitions) invalidates the cache from the edited point onward, which couples release cadence to cost.

Routing half the traffic to a smaller model costing, say, 0.25x per token: with caching, 0.5 x 3.64 + 0.5 x 0.25 x 3.64 = 2.275 units (-51% vs baseline); routing alone gives 2.875 (-37.5%). These savings are only real if quality holds on the routed slice.
practical_answer:
Operational controls and release checks:

1. Tag every model call with tenant, feature, prompt version and model id, and record input, cached-input and output token counts from the response usage data. Without this the 40% cannot be attributed.
2. Track tokens per request per tenant against its own trailing median (for example the last 14 days). Alert when it exceeds 1.5x the median for a day, since a single tenant's behaviour change is the typical anomaly.
3. Give each tenant a daily budget in units with warnings at 80% and 100%. Decide the over-budget behaviour with the product owner: truncate or summarise context, fall back to the small model, queue, or hard stop; do not default silently to a hard stop for a paying customer.
4. Put a cost-per-resolved-ticket metric next to cost-per-request, so a cheaper but less effective path is not rewarded.
5. Release gate for routing or shortened context: run the eval set per slice (by language, intent, tenant tier), canary 5% of traffic with resolution rate, escalation rate and thumbs-down as guardrails, and keep an instant switch back to the large model.
6. Re-run the cost model after each prompt release, because the fixed prefix length and cacheability change with it.
common_mistakes: Assuming cost follows request count, not tokens per request
Putting timestamps or user-specific text at the start of the prompt, which breaks prefix reuse
Routing to a smaller model without a per-slice eval gate and canary
interview_style_note: Does the unit arithmetic correctly, explains why the bill outgrew traffic, and ties cost controls to attribution and a quality gate.

topic: MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
question: A recommender model passes a 5% canary and a 2-week A/B test (click-through +4%, no latency or error regressions) and goes to 100%. Six weeks later, repeat purchases per active user are down 2% against the pre-launch trend while click-through is still up. List the plausible mechanisms, say what evidence would separate them, and explain what release practice would have caught this earlier or made it cheaper to resolve.
answer:
Likely mechanisms, which can overlap: (1) Proxy mismatch. The test optimised click-through, but the goal is repeat purchase. Google's Rules of Machine Learning note that metrics measurable in A/B tests are proxies for longer-term goals, and that launch decisions need several metrics. A model that attracts clicks with narrower or more clickable items can raise clicks and lower later satisfaction. (2) Horizon. If the typical repurchase interval is 3 to 6 weeks, most repeat purchases fall outside a 2-week test window by construction; likewise a canary has to be long enough to be representative (the SRE workbook says so), which is impractical for an outcome metric that takes weeks to mature. (3) Exposure and novelty effects: click-through is still up, so a classic novelty fade in the click lift is not what is observed (check the lift by weeks since launch), but a narrowing of what users see (less diversity, fewer discovery items) can accumulate over weeks and depress later purchases. (4) Confounding by trend or season: the 'down 2% against the pre-launch trend' comparison also contains seasonality, price changes, campaigns and a cohort mix shift. (5) Selection: after launch, the model's own recommendations shape what users buy and what data is logged next.

Separating them: a concurrent control is the cleanest way to answer it. If a holdback group (say 2 to 5% of users kept on the old model if the user base is large enough; size it by a power calculation so it can detect a 2% change in repeat purchases) exists, compare repeat purchase, diversity of items seen and revenue per user between holdback and exposed users from the launch date. Without it, fall back to weaker evidence: difference-in-differences against a segment less exposed to the recommender, same-period-last-year comparison, and cohorts split by exposure date. Check that the metric definition and tracking did not change at the same time. What separates them: a repeat-purchase gap between holdback and exposed users points to the model (proxy mismatch, or narrowing if item diversity also fell); the same dip in both groups points to season or cohort mix; a gap opening only after the test's 2-week horizon shows in cohort curves by weeks since launch.

Practice that would have caught this: a pre-agreed long-term guardrail (repeat purchase or a validated surrogate) with a holdback kept for the horizon that metric needs, the rollout kept reversible by a flag, and a review date. Cost of the holdback is the lost uplift on that slice; it buys the ability to measure the long-term effect. If the holdback shows a real harm, roll back or retune the objective, and consider adding diversity or downstream-conversion terms.
common_mistakes: Concluding the A/B test was wrong because the later metric fell, without checking trend, season and cohort mix
Comparing post-launch numbers only with the pre-launch period instead of a concurrent control
Rolling back at once without a holdback, so the effect of the rollback itself cannot be measured
interview_style_note: Separates proxy mismatch, horizon, novelty and confounding, and insists on a concurrent holdback as the clean counterfactual.

topic: MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
question: A new fraud-scoring model ran in shadow for three weeks: the shadow logged scores for all mirrored requests, 99.9% of them agreed with the expected output computed offline, and the shadow call's p99 latency was 70 ms. After promotion, p99 for the live decision is 400 ms, customers get duplicate 'transaction held' notifications, and live scores for similar customers are noticeably lower than what the shadow had logged. Which properties of the shadow setup could have produced a clean pass that did not predict this, and what would you change in the next shadow?
answer:
The shadow comparison measured whether the model's output agreed with an expectation, not whether the system around it would behave the same once it is the live path. Four properties of a typical shadow setup explain the gap:

1. Latency off the critical path. The shadow call is usually asynchronous, with its own connection pools, thread pool and capacity, and often on a mirrored sample. The 70 ms p99 says nothing about the live path where the call blocks the response, shares pools with the feature fetch, and meets peak-hour queueing. Check whether it included feature retrieval, serialisation, timeout and retry behaviour, and peak load. Under live load, feature-fetch timeouts that fall back to default values, plus client retries, could link all three symptoms (slow, lower scores, duplicates).
2. Side effects were disabled or not exercised. Shadow responses are normally discarded, and the notification, ledger and case-management calls are skipped. In production, every 'hold' decision now triggers those downstream calls, and if the call is retried without an idempotency key you get duplicates. Shadow cannot reveal effects of acting on a decision.
3. Feature freshness differs. If the shadow path read features from a replica, a cache or a snapshot taken at logging time, or the comparison recomputed features offline afterwards, it saw fresher or more complete values than the live path gets at decision time. Late events and missing recent counts then make live feature values differ from what the shadow saw, which can shift live scores (here, lower) without any model change. Log the exact feature values used at serving time and compare those; Google's Rules of Machine Learning (Rule #29) recommend saving the features used at serving time and logging them for use at training time, which also gives you the exact values to compare against offline recomputation.
4. No feedback loop: shadow decisions do not change customer behaviour (customers retry or call support after a hold, fraudsters adapt), so the traffic and load the live model faces differ from the mirrored traffic.

Fixes for the next shadow: run the candidate on the same synchronous code path as the live model (in parallel, with its own timeout and the same pools or an equal share of capacity) at full-peak load; replace downstream services with recording stubs and count the side effects the candidate would have caused, including retries; log serving-time features and compare them to the live model's; then use a canary with guardrails on latency, error and downstream-effect rates before ramping.
common_mistakes: Assuming agreement with offline scores proves the live path will behave the same
Measuring shadow latency on an async path with its own capacity and calling it the live latency
Ignoring downstream effects that only occur when decisions are acted upon

topic: MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
question: An A/B test of a new ranking model (planned 50/50 by user hash) reports +3.1% conversion for treatment. A reviewer notices that assignment counts are 51,000 vs 49,000 users out of 100,000, and that the serving stack has (a) a result cache keyed by (query, locale) with a 10-minute TTL and (b) an online-learning component that updates one shared set of item-popularity weights from clicks in both arms. Explain what each of these can do to the experiment, how you would test for them, and how you would fix the setup.
detailed_answer:
Two separate problems show up in the description.

1. Sample ratio mismatch (SRM). With 100,000 users and a 50/50 plan, you expect 50,000 per arm. The chi-square statistic for 51,000 vs 49,000 is (1000^2/50000) x 2 = 40.0 on 1 degree of freedom, and the p-value is about 2.5e-10 (computed). Chance does not explain that, so something in the pipeline treats the arms differently: for example a crash, redirect, bot filter or logging loss that affects one arm, or assignment happening after an event that differs by arm. Do not interpret the +3.1% until the SRM is explained, because the missing users are rarely missing at random.

2. Interference between arms. The result cache keyed only by (query, locale) means whichever arm populates an entry first determines what the other arm's users receive for 10 minutes, so some control users see treatment rankings and vice versa. The shared online-learning weights mean treatment clicks update the model that also serves control, so the two arms are no longer independent systems; the test then measures a blend, which typically biases the estimated difference towards zero (direction is not guaranteed, for example when the learner favours the arm that generates more clicks). This is the stable-unit-treatment-value problem seen from the operations side. Hidden Technical Debt in ML Systems notes that a model may directly influence the selection of its own future training data; an online learner shared across arms is a version of that.

Fixes: include the experiment arm in the cache key (or bypass caching for the test); keep separate learner state per arm, or freeze learning during the test and compare fixed models; log both the assigned and the actually served variant per request and analyse by served arm only as a diagnostic; run an A/A test through the same stack to see whether the pipeline produces SRM or a non-zero difference with identical arms.
practical_answer:
Checklist for analysing a suspect test, in order:

- Run the SRM check first. Computed: observed 51,000 vs 49,000 users, expected 50,000 each, chi-square 40.0 on 1 d.f., p about 2.5e-10. Treat any p below a strict threshold (many teams use something like 0.001) as 'results invalid until explained'.
- Break the counts by day, platform, country and entry point; the segment where the ratio is off often names the cause (for example an app version that crashes only in treatment).
- Look for an arm leak: for a sample of requests compare the assigned arm with the variant recorded on the served response. A non-trivial share of mismatches indicates cache or routing contamination.
- Run an A/A test (both arms get the old model) through the same cache and learner. If it shows SRM or a repeatable significant difference between identical arms (a single A/A run will show p < 0.05 about 5% of the time by chance), the platform is the problem, not the model.
- Decide the design: per-arm cache namespaces and per-arm (or frozen) learner state. If the learner must be shared in production, accept that the test measures the new model inside the shared system and say so.
- Re-run, then compare against the planned 50/50: a matching ratio and a null A/A are the conditions for reading the conversion lift.
common_mistakes: Reporting the +3.1% and treating the 51,000 vs 49,000 split as harmless noise
Assuming interference can only inflate the lift; it can also dilute or distort it
Keying a cache without the experiment arm
interview_style_note: Recognises SRM as a validity gate, identifies two operational interference channels, and proposes tests (A/A, assigned-vs-served) and architectural fixes.

topic: MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
question: A product-search ranker trained on click logs raises offline AUC from 0.78 to 0.81 on a held-out week of logged impressions, but the online A/B test shows conversion of 3.10% vs 3.09% (not significant, with enough traffic that a 1% relative change would have been detectable). Give the explanations specific to logged-data evaluation that you would investigate, in the order you would check them, and how you would change the offline evaluation so it predicts the online result better.
answer:
Offline AUC measures how well the model separates clicked from non-clicked impressions in logged data. That is not the same as improving what users do when the new model controls the page, and several mechanisms can open that gap.

1. Logged data come from the old policy. Items shown high up got more attention, so click labels mix item relevance with position and exposure. A new model can raise AUC partly by learning position-correlated features (item popularity under the old ranker, previous rank, cache or slot id) that predict clicks in the logs but do not move users' behaviour when the new model reorders items. The check is to compute AUC within position buckets, or on a small randomised-ranking slice if you have one, and to see whether AUC rises there.
2. Selection bias: the logs contain only items the old system chose to show. The new model is evaluated and trained on that subset but must rank the whole candidate set live, including items never seen in training (a different distribution). Hidden Technical Debt in ML Systems describes the related direct feedback loop, where a model influences the selection of its own training data; exploration or randomised-ranking traffic is one mitigation (Sculley et al. also mention isolating part of the data from the model's influence); counterfactual evaluation (inverse-propensity weighting) needs known or estimated propensities: for item exposure the logging policy must have been stochastic with recorded propensities, since items the old ranker never showed cannot be reweighted into the data (position-bias propensities can instead be estimated from a small randomisation experiment).
3. Label and objective mismatch. AUC on clicks does not imply conversion; clickbait-style items raise click prediction without improving purchases. Pooled AUC also mixes between-query and within-query comparisons and weighs the whole list equally, so a model can gain AUC in the tail without improving ranks 1 to 5, where the outcome is decided. Use a top-of-list metric (nDCG@5, or conversion-weighted) offline.
4. Training-serving skew and saturation. Log the features used at serving time (Rules of Machine Learning rule 29) and compare them, and the scores they produce, with the offline pipeline on the same examples (rule 37), and check whether the conversion funnel simply has little headroom at the ranking step.

Plan, in the order of items 1 to 4 (the skew check is cheap, so start it in parallel): reproduce the offline metric per position, replay with propensity weighting where propensities were logged, re-score with nDCG@5 or a conversion-weighted metric, check skew by logging serving-time features, then validate with a small online test using a primary metric tied to conversion.
common_mistakes: Assuming a higher AUC on any held-out data implies a better ranking in production
Evaluating on impressions produced by the old ranker and ignoring exposure and position
Using AUC alone when the business outcome depends on the top few ranks
interview_style_note: Explains why offline AUC on logged clicks can mislead and proposes concrete diagnostics (per-position AUC, propensity weighting, top-rank metrics).

topic: MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
question: A real-time pricing model is served from an online store, while training features come from an offline pipeline. You are asked to build a consistency check that would have caught an incident where a deploy silently shifted one windowed count by one. Design the check: what you log at serving time, how and when you recompute offline, how you define tolerances for different feature types, how you use timestamps to root-cause a mismatch, and what you alert on. Show the comparison as SQL that you have executed.
detailed_answer:
Design in four parts.

Log. For a sample of live requests (say 1%; at 2 million requests/day this is 20,000 comparisons), write the exact feature values the model received, with request id, entity id, served-at timestamp, model version and feature-pipeline version. Saving the features used at serving time is the approach Google's Rules of Machine Learning recommend, and doing it for a small fraction of examples is acceptable.

Recompute. A scheduled job, run after the lateness allowance has elapsed (for example hourly with a lag of a few hours), recomputes the same features with the offline pipeline, as of served_at (point-in-time, using only data that was available then, or with an explicit lateness allowance). Recomputing 'as of now' will report differences that are just late-arriving events and deletions, which swamps real bugs.

Compare with per-feature tolerances. Integers, ids and categories: exact. Floats: absolute plus relative tolerance (to absorb floating-point and rounding order). Windowed counts that depend on event lateness: keep the tolerance at zero (a non-zero tolerance would hide the off-by-one incident in the question) and make the recomputation point-in-time on arrival time, using only events that had arrived by served_at, which needs an ingestion timestamp. If the offline source has no arrival time, late events make offline counts exceed served ones, so compare only features computed over windows that had already closed, and were past the lateness allowance, when the request was served (for example the previous complete day; a rolling window ending at served_at never qualifies, so there an ingestion timestamp is needed), and track the late-event rate separately. NULL versus non-NULL is always a mismatch. Requests with no recomputation are tracked separately.

Root-cause with time. Aggregate mismatch rate by feature and hour (and by model or pipeline version). A step beginning at a deploy time points to a code change; a daily spike at a fixed hour to a batch job or cache expiry; mismatches concentrated in new entities to cold-start defaults. Alert on a mismatch rate above a threshold you choose per feature, with the sample size in mind: if all 20,000 comparisons match, the 95% upper bound on the true mismatch rate is about 3/20,000 = 0.015% (the rule of three). The ML Test Score lists 'Training and serving features compute the same values' as a monitoring test.
practical_answer:
Executed example of the comparison query (SQLite dialect, run with Python's sqlite3 on a small in-memory dataset). It reports, per hour and feature, how many sampled requests had no offline recomputation and how many differed beyond that feature's tolerance. Clean hours are filtered out.

```python
import sqlite3

SQL = """
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:00', s.served_at) AS hour,
       s.feature,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       SUM(CASE WHEN r.request_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS not_recomputed,
       SUM(CASE WHEN r.request_id IS NOT NULL AND (
             (s.value IS NULL) <> (r.value IS NULL)
             OR ABS(s.value - r.value) > t.abs_tol + t.rel_tol * ABS(r.value)
           ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS mismatched
FROM served s
JOIN tolerances t ON t.feature = s.feature
LEFT JOIN recomputed r ON r.request_id = s.request_id AND r.feature = s.feature
GROUP BY hour, s.feature
HAVING mismatched > 0 OR not_recomputed > 0
ORDER BY hour, s.feature;
"""


def consistency_report(conn):
    return conn.execute(SQL).fetchall()
```

On the test data (10 requests per hour, with a deploy-time fault in 4 of the 10 in the 14:00 hour, plus one NULL-served value and one request without recomputation), the query returned: ('2026-03-01 14:00', 'avg_basket', 11, 0, 1) and ('2026-03-01 14:00', 'orders_24h', 11, 1, 4). Reading it: in the 14:00 hour, 4 of the 10 recomputed orders_24h values were off by one and one more request had no recomputation, and one avg_basket was NULL when served but 25.0 offline. The 13:00 hour does not appear because its avg_basket differences (0.004) are within tolerance and the other values match. A mismatch that begins in the hour after a deploy is where to start reading the diff. Caveats: the inner join to tolerances silently drops any feature that has no tolerance row, so require one per logged feature, and recomputed must be unique per (request_id, feature) or the counts double. The comparison is also numeric only: for text ids or categories ABS(s.value - r.value) is 0, so a changed value would be reported as a match. Encode such features as integers (for example a dictionary index) or add a null-safe exact test such as (t.abs_tol = 0 AND t.rel_tol = 0 AND s.value IS NOT r.value) before relying on the query for them.
common_mistakes: Recomputing offline 'as of now', so late events appear as mismatches
Using one global tolerance for ids, counts and floats
Comparing only aggregate distributions and missing row-level mismatches
interview_style_note: Designs a row-level, point-in-time consistency check with typed tolerances and uses timestamps to attribute mismatches to deploys or batch jobs.

topic: MLOps case studies, deployment tests (canary/shadow/A-B) and online/offline consistency incidents
question: Your team has a quarter to spend and must choose between (A) building a new model and (B) investing in monitoring and feature-consistency checks for the existing one. Hypothetical numbers: the model influences about 24 million per year of margin. A: offline estimate +1.5% relative uplift, past launches realised about half of the offline uplift, cost 5 engineer-months at 20,000 per engineer-month. B: history shows about 3 silent degradations a year, each costing about 2% of the model's margin until noticed, which takes about 6 weeks today; with monitoring about 3 days. B costs 3 engineer-months to build plus about 3 engineer-months of ongoing care per year. Work out the expected value of each, show the sensitivity to the assumptions you trust least, and give a recommendation.
detailed_answer:
All figures are hypothetical.

Option A, the new model. Margin influenced by the model: 24 million/year. Offline estimate +1.5% relative; past launches realised about half of the offline uplift, so the expected gain is 0.015 x 0.5 x 24M = 180,000/year. Cost: 5 engineer-months x 20,000 = 100,000. Expected net about +80,000 in year 1. This is sensitive to the realisation factor: at 25% realisation the gain is 90,000 and the net is about -10,000. You learn the realised gain only after an online test.

Option B, monitoring and consistency checks. History: about 3 silent degradations per year, each costing about 2% of the model's margin until noticed; detection currently takes about 6 weeks. Reading the 2% as the share of margin lost while an incident lasts, one incident costs 24M x 0.02 x 6/52 = 55,385. With monitoring, detection in about 3 days costs 24M x 0.02 x 3/365 = 3,945. Saving per incident about 51,440 (assuming monitoring catches every incident within 3 days and reading the 2% as a loss rate while the incident lasts; under the alternative reading in the practical answer, B wins by a wide margin); 3 incidents save about 154,300/year. Cost: 3 engineer-months to build (60,000) plus about 3 engineer-months of ongoing care per year (60,000), so year 1 is 120,000 and net about +34,300; later years net about +94,300. Break-even in year 1 is about 2.3 incidents per year (120,000 / 51,440).

Reading the numbers. On these assumptions A has the higher expected net in year 1 (about 80,000 vs 34,300) and, if the gain persists, in later years too (the build cost is not repeated), but its realised gain is uncertain until an online test; B's net swings similarly with the incident rate, yet it is insurance against a loss you currently cannot see. Two points matter more than the arithmetic. First, B also enables A: without serving-time feature logging and quality monitoring you cannot tell whether the new model's gain is real or an incident erased it, and the new model inherits the same blind spots. Second, the incident rate and cost per incident come from a small sample (three events) and should be treated as ranges. Hidden Technical Debt notes the external world is rarely stable, so do not assume the incident rate falls by itself.

A defensible recommendation is to run the cheapest high-value monitoring first (training-serving feature consistency and staleness checks, both monitoring tests in the ML Test Score, plus prediction-distribution or prediction-bias checks as discussed in Hidden Technical Debt) and to ship the model after it, with the monitoring used to read the A/B result.
practical_answer:
Sensitivity table to bring to the decision meeting (same hypothetical inputs):

- Option A, realised fraction of offline uplift: 25% -> gross 90,000, net -10,000; 50% -> gross 180,000, net 80,000; 75% -> gross 270,000, net 170,000.
- Option B, silent incidents per year (saving about 51,440 each, year-1 cost 120,000): 1 -> net -68,600; 2 -> net -17,100; 3 -> net +34,300; 4 -> net +85,800.
- Alternative reading of the 2%: if it is the whole pre-detection cost of one incident rather than a rate, one incident costs 24M x 0.02 = 480,000 and the monitored version 24M x 0.02 x 3/42 = 34,300, so the saving is about 445,700 per incident and B wins by a wide margin; ask how the 2% was measured.
- If the monitoring cost in later years is only the 60,000 ongoing part, break-even falls to about 1.2 incidents per year (60,000 / 51,440).

Questions that move the decision: How was '3 incidents a year' counted, and how many were found only by customers? What does a 2% margin loss look like in practice, and is it plausible that the new model would be hit by the same incidents? Can the first slice of B (for example the serving-feature consistency check) be done in one engineer-month and cover most of the historical incidents? If yes, do it first and treat the remainder of B and A as the next two decisions.
common_mistakes: Comparing only the headline uplift of the model with the build cost of monitoring and ignoring avoided losses
Presenting point estimates without sensitivity to the realisation factor and incident rate
Treating monitoring and the new model as independent when monitoring is needed to read the new model's result
interview_style_note: Builds a simple expected-value model from stated assumptions, tests it with sensitivity, and ties the recommendation to risk, variance and sequencing.
